title: full text analysis
text:
This project analyzes tweets posted by former President Barack Obama using data from the Barack Obama Twitter Archive. The goal is to explore what topics received attention, how messaging changed over time, and how political communication was shaped by hashtags and language patterns. I focus on three linguistic features: references to America, hashtag usage, and mentions of policy areas.
The frequency of Obama’s tweets changes over time. There are visible spikes during major political moments such as elections, major speeches, and legislative pushes. This suggests Twitter served as a strategic communication tool rather than a constant personal feed, activity increased when public engagement was most important.









Hashtags help reveal Obama’s messaging priorities. The most common hashtags include policy topics such as #obamacare, #education, and #climatechange, emphasizing the administration’s key legislative and advocacy themes. Their high frequency indicates that social media played a role in promoting government initiatives and shaping public conversation around policy values.









I used regular expressions to automatically detect whether tweets contained certain political themes. For example, searching for “america” and “american” helps identify nationalistic messaging, while hashtag extraction highlights how Obama’s team used platform-specific tools to coordinate public conversation. The policy-related keyword search allows me to isolate communication focused on healthcare, education, climate issues, and the economy, topics central to Obama’s presidency.
Data Source:
The data used in this analysis come from the Barack Obama Twitter Archive, collected and published by the U.S. National Archives and Records Administration (NARA).
Available at: https://github.com/ObamaWhiteHouse/twitter-archive

title: visual inference lineup — global temperature trends
text:
Overview
In this project, I looked at whether there’s a real upward trend in global temperature over time. The data come from the NOAA Global Land–Ocean Temperature Index (GISTEMP).
To test the trend, I used something called a visual inference lineup. Basically, we compare the real data to a bunch of “fake” plots where the data have been shuffled. If people can spot the real plot, that means there’s likely a true trend.

title: visual inference lineup — global temperature trends
text:
The Real Data

ggplot(global, aes(x = Year, y = temp_anomaly)) +
geom_line(color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1.1) +
geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
labs(
title = "Global Temperature Anomalies (1880–2023)",
subtitle = "Data Source: NOAA / NASA GISTEMP",
x = "Year",
y = "Temperature Anomaly (°C)"
) +
theme_minimal()

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









This line chart shows how each year’s average global temperature compares to a long-term baseline. It looks like the temperatures are going up over time, but we’ll check if that pattern could just happen by chance.

title: visual inference lineup — global temperature trends
text:
Simulating the Null Hypothesis
If there’s no real trend, the temperature values shouldn’t be linked to the year. To simulate this, I wrote a function that randomly mixes up the temperature values and makes a new plot.

simulate_null_plot <- function(data) {
shuffled <- data %>%
mutate(temp_anomaly = sample(temp_anomaly))

ggplot(shuffled, aes(x = Year, y = temp_anomaly)) +
geom_line(color = "grey50", alpha = 0.8) +
geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linetype = "dotted") +
theme_minimal() +
labs(x = "Year", y = "Temp Anomaly (°C)")
}

title: visual inference lineup — global temperature trends
text:
Creating the Lineup
Now I use map() to make several of these shuffled plots, then add the real one to compare them all side by side.

set.seed(42)

# Create 5 null datasets

null_dfs <- map(1:5, ~global %>%
mutate(temp_anomaly = sample(temp_anomaly), lineup_id = paste0("Null ", .x)))

# Real data labeled separately

real_df <- global %>% mutate(lineup_id = "Real Data")

# Combine all datasets

lineup_df <- bind_rows(null_dfs, real_df)

# Plot all lineups using facet_wrap

ggplot(lineup_df, aes(x = Year, y = temp_anomaly)) +
geom_line(color = "steelblue", alpha = 0.8) +
geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black", linetype = "dotted") +
facet_wrap(~lineup_id, ncol = 3) +
theme_minimal() +
labs(
title = "Visual Inference Lineup: Is There a Trend in Global Temperatures?",
subtitle = "Each panel shows a dataset with years vs. temperature anomalies — only one is real.",
x = "Year",
y = "Temperature Anomaly (°C)"
)

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

title: visual inference lineup — global temperature trends
text:
What it means
If people can easily pick out the real data from the shuffled ones, that’s strong visual evidence that there’s a true trend. Even without running a formal test, the real plot stands out with a steady rise over time. That makes it clear that global temperatures are really increasing — not just random noise.

title: male vs. female tv shows ratings
text:
Step 1: Research Question and Context
In this project, I investigate whether IMDb ratings for TV shows differ between male-identifying and female-identifying reviewers in the larger population of TV viewers, not just in this dataset. The “IMDb_Economist_tv_ratings.csv” dataset comes from The Economist (via TidyTuesday Week 2, 2019) and includes TV show titles, average IMDb ratings, and gender-split rating data.
We want to understand whether the small differences observed in this dataset could reasonably occur from random chance alone. To answer this, we simulate a world where gender has no role in how people rate TV shows. Under that null hypothesis, any difference we see in average ratings would simply be due to natural variability from sample to sample.
Our goal:
“Is the difference we observe in our dataset larger than we would normally expect if the underlying rating tendency were the same for everyone?”


Step 2: Setup and Data Cleaning


[1] -0.03695642


[1] 0.9056











Step 3: Interpretation:
The histogram shows what differences in average ratings we would expect just by chance if gender were unrelated to TV show ratings in the broader viewer population. The orange dashed line marks the difference we observed in the dataset. Because the observed value lies near the center of the simulated null distribution, differences of this size would be very common even if gender truly had no effect. Therefore, our observed difference is not unusual under the null hypothesis.


Step 4: Conclusions
This permutation test evaluates whether the difference in TV show ratings between male and female reviewers seen in this dataset is larger than what would be expected from normal random variation. Because the observed difference aligns closely with the null distribution, we do not have evidence that rating tendencies differ by gender in the broader population of IMDb users. This does not prove that gender will never matter, rather, based on the dataset available, any differences we observe could easily be explained by chance alone.


References

title: ethics and power
text:
Ethical Dilemma: Amazon’s AI Hiring Algorithm and Bias Against Women

Scenario Overview
In 2018, Reuters reporter Jeffrey Dastin revealed that Amazon had built an internal machine-learning hiring tool intended to automatically score job applicants and identify the most promising candidates. According to Dastin (2018), the system was trained on ten years of past résumés, most of which came from men, reflecting the male, dominated tech workforce. As a result, the algorithm learned to penalize résumés that included the word “women’s” (as in “women’s chess club” or “women’s coding team”) and even downgraded graduates of all-women colleges. Amazon attempted to remove biased rules, but the system continued finding proxy variables for gender. Eventually, the company scrapped the tool.
The data science component of the story is the machine-learning model trained on historical résumé data (Dastin, 2018; Hao, 2019). The ethical dilemma is that the model reproduced, and in some cases amplified, existing gender biases in hiring, raising questions about fairness, accountability, transparency, and the moral responsibility of companies deploying automated decision systems. Because Amazon never used the tool in actual hiring decisions, the harm was limited internally, but the case reveals how easily data-driven systems can encode systemic discrimination.


1. Permission Structure for Using the Data
Dastin (2018) reported that Amazon fed the AI system thousands of historic résumés submitted to the company. These résumés were provided by job applicants for the explicit purpose of being evaluated by humans—not to train machine-learning systems. Although Amazon legally owned the résumé data once it was submitted, the ethical permission structure is more complicated. Applicants did not meaningfully consent to have their résumés repurposed for experimental algorithms. Even though Amazon stayed within its legal rights, the company failed to acknowledge the difference between legal data use and ethically appropriate data use, especially when the outcomes influence employment opportunities.


2. Consent and Whether Participants Knew Their Data Would Be Used in Research
Neither Dastin (2018) nor MIT Technology Review found any indication that job applicants were told their résumés would be used to train or test AI models. Dastin (2018) emphasized that the system was “secret” within Amazon, with even some internal staff unaware of its scope. MIT Technology Review later noted that many companies assume that submitted résumés are “fair game” for internal analytics, but applicants rarely understand how their data will be used or what new inferences will be drawn from it. Because machine-learning research can generate unforeseeable new predictions, such as inferred gender or inferred likelihood of job performance, informed consent in the traditional sense was impossible. Applicants could not meaningfully consent to uses that did not exist when they applied.


3. Were the Data Representative, and Should We Analyze Data If We Don’t Understand Its Origins?
Dastin (2018) made clear that the training data consisted of ten years of résumés submitted to Amazon, most from men. This is a classic example of non-representative training data. Because the tech industry has long been male-dominated, the “successful” résumés overwhelmingly came from men, and the algorithm learned a simple pattern: men were more likely to be hired in the past, therefore male-like résumés should be scored higher. The data were not representative of the applicant pool Amazon should want, nor of the qualified labor market. This shows why it is dangerous to build models without deeply examining how the data were collected and what biases they embed. Training on biased historical data essentially automates past discrimination.


4. Was the Data Used in Unintended Ways Compared to the Original Context?
The résumés (i.e., the data) were also used in unintended ways in the following: they were originally sent in to get a job, they were not originally sent in to train an algorithm. (Dastin, 2018; Hao, 2019)
MIT Technology Review highlighted how Amazon’s system drifted away from evaluating skills and instead learned to detect gender-related patterns. The original intent was to build an efficient tool to identify good candidates. Instead, the model used résumé patterns as proxies for gender, creating unintended discrimination (Hao, 2019). Features like participation in “women’s activities” or attendance at women’s colleges were never intended to harm candidates, but the algorithm treated them as negative signals simply because of patterns in historical data (Dastin, 2018). This is a clear example of “function creep,” where data collected for one purpose (screening) evolves into unintended, ethically problematic inference (gender classification).


Why This Matters: Who Benefits and Who Is Harmed?
The Amazon hiring algorithm matters because it shows how data science can shift power and responsibility in high-stakes decisions. Amazon potentially benefited by automating hiring, reducing recruiter workload, and building proprietary AI tools. But women and other underrepresented groups were disproportionately harmed, as the system learned to filter them out. These harms were not the result of malicious intent, but of historical bias baked into training data, combined with insufficient oversight and ethical review. The ethical violations served interests of efficiency and corporate innovation, not fairness. The case raises the broader moral question: Who is responsible when an automated system discriminates the engineers, the managers, the company, or the data itself? As this example shows, the responsibility lies with the organization that chooses to deploy (or even experiment with) algorithmic hiring without proper safeguards, transparency, or accountability frameworks.
Dastin, J. (2018, October 10). Amazon scraps secret AI recruiting tool that showed bias against women. Reuters. https://www.reuters.com/article/us-amazon-com-jobs-automation-insight-idUSKCN1MK08G
Hao, K. (2019, February 4). Amazon’s AI hiring tool still has lessons for companies today. MIT Technology Review. https://www.technologyreview.com/2019/02/04/137783/amazon-ai-hiring-bias-women/

title: sql traffic stops
text:
Introduction
In this project I compare traffic stops in California, Washington, and Oregon using data from the Stanford Open Policing Project. I focus on three questions: (1) how the number of stops has changed over time in each state, (2) how often searches occur for different racial groups, and (3) whether searches for different racial groups are equally likely to find contraband (hit rates) in each state. All data wrangling is done using SQL; R is used only for visualization and formatting.

Analysis 1









Overall, California has many more traffic stops than Washington and Oregon each year. California has over five million stops annually in this period, while Washington has around one million and Oregon has fewer than half a million. California experiences a noticeable decline in stops after 2011, while Washington and Oregon remain relatively stable across 2010–2013.
These patterns could reflect differences in enforcement strategies, driving behavior, or recordingpractices across states. Because each state varies in how and when they began contributing data, some of the differences in trends may arise from the availability and completeness of the data itself rather than only real-world changes in policing.


Analysis 2









This figure shows the proportion of stops that involve a search by race for California and Washington since 2015. In both states, Black and Hispanic drivers are searched at higher rates than white and Asian/Pacific Islander drivers. Washington tends to have slightly higher search rates across most racial groups than California. These differences suggest that search practices are not experienced equally across racial groups or across states.


Analysis 3









This plot compares the number of stops by month for California and Washington. Both states show more traffic stops in the summer months and fewer in the winter, but California has far more stops overall in every month. The similar seasonal pattern suggests that factors like weather, travel, or enforcement cycles affect both states in roughly the same way, even though the total volume of stops is very different.


Conclusion
In this project, I used SQL to wrangle traffic stop data from California, Washington, and Oregon in order to compare patterns over time, across races, and across the calendar year. The first analysis showed that California has far more traffic stops than Washington and Oregon, as Washington and Oregon remain relatively stable across 2010–2013. The second analysis found that Black and Hispanic drivers are searched at higher rates than white and Asian/Pacific Islander drivers in both states, with Washington generally having slightly higher search rates overall. Finally, the third analysis showed that both states have more stops in summer and fewer in winter, suggesting similar seasonal dynamics despite very different total volumes. Together, these results illustrate how SQL can be used to explore large policing datasets and highlight differences in traffic stop practices across states and groups.


Source
Data used in this project come from the Stanford Open Policing Project: https://openpolicing.stanford.edu/data/

title: diving
text:
Diving + Shiny!
This project uses Data Science and interactive graphics to explore my performance as a springboard diver. Data comes directly from my DiveMeets profile and includes:

Dive codes
Dive descriptions
High score and average score
How many times I’ve competed each dive
Dive group (Forward, Back, Reverse, Inward, Twist)

The project uses:

R web scraping (rvest)
Data cleaning and wrangling (dplyr)
Shiny interactive visualization (ggplot + reactive filtering)



Step 1 - Import and Scrape My Dive Stats
I read data directly from DiveMeets using rvest, which converts HTML table data into an R data frame.


Step 2 - Select and Clean the Dive Table
DiveMeets had some formatting quirks, so I:

removed repeated header rows
corrected misplaced score columns
kept only useful columns



Step 3 - Add Dive Group Categories
Every dive code’s first digit tells the group:

1 = Forward, 2 = Back, 3 = Reverse, 4 = Inward, 5 = Twist


Extra Credit: Shiny Interactive Plot!
I expanded this project with Shiny, which updates the visualization instantly based on user input.

Users can choose a dive group and explore my average scores dynamically.
This demonstrates:

The Shiny UI + server reactive framework
Interactive filtering of my real athletic stats
ggplot updating automatically based on selections



Shiny applications not supported in static R Markdown documents


Note: The Shiny application runs interactively in RStudio using shinyApp(ui, server) at the bottom of this document. Because Shiny is not supported in static HTML knitting, the interactive plot does not appear here, but is fully functional when running the document in RStudio.
